stories.headline: Three AI-native companies use agents to streamline onboarding, account management, and integrations
stories.dek: Basis, Clay, and Exa Labs show how enterprise teams can embed AI agents into core business processes to reduce manual work.
stories.summary:
Basis, Clay, and Exa Labs each deployed AI agents to automate labor-intensive workflows that directly affect customer experience and team efficiency. Basis used agents to speed up customer onboarding by handling repetitive setup and qualification tasks. Clay built agents to manage account lifecycles, automating outreach and status tracking for sales operations. Exa Labs created agents that streamline developer integrations, reducing the friction new users encounter when connecting the platform to their systems.

These aren't experimental projects—all three companies integrated agents into production workflows that customers and internal teams rely on daily. The implementations show a pattern: identify a workflow where humans currently spend time on predictable, rule-based tasks; deploy an agent to handle the routine work; free the team to focus on judgment calls and relationship building. Each case illustrates that AI agent capability has matured past chatbots into tools that can be embedded as operating functions, not just interfaces.
stories.why_it_matters: Your consulting work is built on translating AI capability into business outcome—these three cases offer concrete teaching examples of agent-first workflow design that your clients face. The specificity (onboarding, account management, integrations) means you can use them in workshops to show how agent reasoning replaces manual task sequences, not just to support human decisions. For your own India ecosystem tracking: watch whether Indian SaaS and services firms adopt similar patterns, and where they struggle to deploy agents into operations.
stories.potential_use: Pull these three cases as a workshop framework: define a client workflow, map the manual steps, model where an agent adds value vs. where human judgment is essential, then prototype the agent integration. Use them as reference designs when consulting on enterprise AI agent deployment. Also a teaching lens for your own AI expertise: study how each company designed the agent's scope to fit organizational responsibility, not just technical capability.

sources.title: How AI-native companies turn workflows into operating capability

stories.headline: Gilbert + Tobin shows how law firms scale AI with CEO backing and governance frameworks
stories.dek: The Australian law firm deployed ChatGPT Enterprise and Codex across the organization by anchoring implementation in executive commitment and clear accountability structures.
stories.summary: Gilbert + Tobin, a major Australian law firm, has successfully deployed ChatGPT Enterprise and Codex organization-wide by building AI adoption on three pillars: explicit CEO commitment to the initiative, formal governance structures that define who decides what and when, and clear human accountability for outcomes. This approach allowed the firm to move beyond pilot projects to genuine enterprise-scale usage across teams and practice areas. The model prioritizes neither moving fast without guardrails nor building so much oversight that adoption stalls—instead, governance and execution happen in parallel, with decision-making authority clearly assigned so that teams know what they can and cannot do with the tools. The case illustrates how professional services firms, which typically operate in heavily regulated environments and work with sensitive client data, can establish the institutional discipline needed to manage AI risk while still capturing productivity gains from these tools.
stories.why_it_matters: For AI consultancy work, this shows a replicable playbook: enterprise AI implementation depends less on tool sophistication than on governance design and executive visibility. For your workshops, it's a concrete example of how organizations move from AI pilots to institutionalized use—something most of your clients will need to navigate. It also reflects how professional services firms specifically approach AI, which is a distinct use case from tech companies and relevant if you're advising law or consulting practices on their AI strategy.
stories.potential_use: This case works well as a workshop module on governance design—use it to walk through how to structure accountability in distributed AI adoption. For consulting engagements, you can reference how Gilbert + Tobin handled the tension between enabling teams and maintaining control, especially relevant if your clients operate in regulated industries. Also a useful reference point for how Indian law and professional services firms might approach similar scaling challenges.

stories.headline: OpenAI adds EHR integration to ChatGPT for clinical use
stories.dek: Healthcare organizations can now connect patient records and research data directly into ChatGPT via trusted integrations.
stories.summary: OpenAI has released a feature allowing healthcare organizations to connect electronic health record systems and other industry data sources directly to ChatGPT. This allows clinicians to pull patient context, medical research, and other healthcare information into their ChatGPT sessions while maintaining security and data integrity. The integration is designed for organizations that need to give their clinical teams access to patient records and supporting evidence in a single interface, without manually copying data across systems. The move positions ChatGPT as an interface layer for existing healthcare IT infrastructure rather than a replacement for it.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a concrete example of enterprise AI integration with regulated, sensitive data systems. For Applicative AI, it surfaces the real compliance and architecture questions your healthcare clients will face: how to connect legacy EHR systems to modern AI tools, how to maintain audit trails and access controls, and how to handle HIPAA and patient consent. It also demonstrates the shift from "AI replaces tools" to "AI coordinates between tools"—a framing that's increasingly relevant to your consulting work.
stories.potential_use: Use this as a case study in workshops on enterprise AI integration: walk through the data flow, security model, and organizational barriers to deployment. It's also a concrete opening for healthcare sector consulting work—many organizations have ChatGPT but haven't figured out safe EHR connectivity yet.

sources.title: Healthcare organizations can now connect EHR and additional industry data to ChatGPT

stories.headline: AIR raises $50M to vet AI agents and their skills at scale
stories.dek: The startup's platform discovers running agents and continuously re-inspects every skill and tool they access, blocking unauthorized connections.
stories.summary: Israeli cybersecurity veterans Yair Saban and Niv Hoffman launched AIR to address a specific operational gap: as companies deploy AI agents with broad system access, the skills, plugins, and MCP servers those agents use lack the kind of security controls that desktop drivers or OS-level code got years ago. AIR's platform maps all agents running inside a company's environment, continuously vets the third-party tools and add-ons they load against a maintained whitelist, and blocks unsafe interactions. The startup currently filters out roughly 27% of the add-ons and skills it finds online. It has already signed more than 20 customers, with roughly a quarter being large enterprises, and has seen strongest adoption in financial services and pharma—industries with strict regulatory requirements. Sequoia led a $10M first round and Greenoaks led a $40M second round, both closing within weeks of each other, with notable angels including Cognition's Zach Frankel and Wiz co-founder Yinon Costica.
stories.why_it_matters: For a consulting firm building enterprise AI programs, agent governance is now a concrete operational problem rather than theoretical risk. AIR's entry—and the $250M+ already raised across competing products like Zenity and Noma—signals that enterprises view agent skill vetting as table stakes, not optional. Understanding this defense layer helps consultants design more defensible agent deployments and articulate ROI around governance infrastructure to clients.
stories.potential_use: Workshop angle: Use AIR's discovery and enforcement model as a case study for designing guardrails into agent systems—what discovery looks like, how to construct a skill allowlist, and how to implement runtime controls. For consulting services, position agent governance assessment (discovering undocumented agents, auditing skill usage) as a pre-deployment engagement, differentiating from pure security vendors by integrating it into architecture planning.

sources.title: AIR raises $50M to help companies vet the skills and add-ons AI agents use

stories.headline: Gemini adds agentic video understanding, cuts token costs by 66%
stories.dek: The new capability lets the model actively decide which frames, audio, and transcript moments to examine rather than processing video at fixed frame rates.
stories.summary:
Google DeepMind launched agentic video understanding across Gemini 3.7 Flash, 3.6 Flash, and 3.5 Flash-Lite. The feature shifts video analysis from static processing—where models ingest content at a fixed frame rate—to an agent-directed approach where Gemini dynamically decides what to examine, at what speed, and through which modality (frames, audio, or transcript). The model fetches only the relevant segments rather than processing the entire stream.

Benchmarks show the efficiency is substantial: token consumption drops by up to 88%, analysis costs fall by up to 66%, and accuracy improves by up to 7%. The gains are most pronounced on long-form video, where static processing forces a tradeoff between high token costs and dropping critical details. Gemini 3.7 Flash lands at the accuracy-to-cost frontier compared to other tested models.

Concrete capabilities include sub-second moment retrieval for precise video editing, long-form search across multi-hour recordings, higher-resolution anomaly detection on interesting segments, and accurate action counting over time. The feature is available now via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, with no additional fee beyond standard token pricing. Rollout to the Gemini app is planned soon, and the capability will power YouTube's "Ask YouTube" feature.
stories.why_it_matters: This extends agent reasoning to multimodal analysis at scale—a key frontier beyond text-only AI. For your consultancy, it demonstrates how agentic loops reduce token waste and unlock practical workflows (video QA, automated editing, anomaly detection) that would be prohibitively expensive with naive approaches. The architecture—agents deciding what to sample rather than processing linearly—is a teaching pattern worth extracting: it applies beyond video to any high-dimensional input. For India's ecosystem, this puts open-weight video models and edge-based video analysis on the roadmap.
stories.potential_use: Workshop angle: build a demo showing the difference between static and agentic video processing—have participants write queries and see token usage drop. Consulting angle: audit clients' video analysis workflows for token waste and refit them with agentic sampling. Learning angle: study the internal tool invocation pattern—how Gemini decides to load specific video segments—as a case study in agent design beyond text retrieval-augmented generation.

stories.headline: Anthropic launches Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with zero-data retention
stories.dek: Data stays in customer-controlled cloud infrastructure while Anthropic runs automated detection for misuse across sessions and accounts.
stories.summary:
Anthropic announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), a system that resolves a tension enterprise security teams face: frontier models need 30-day data retention to detect sophisticated misuse patterns across sessions and accounts, but regulated companies resist giving vendors access to sensitive data. EFS stores activity logs in the customer's own cloud infrastructure—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage—under encryption keys the customer controls, while Anthropic runs automated detection on that data for threats like stolen credentials, cyberattacks, and attempts to develop harmful capabilities.

The company developed this in collaboration with over 100 enterprises including members of the ARC (Analysis and Resilience Center for Systemic Risk), which includes security leaders from Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. Customer teams handle all human review; Anthropic staff have no access. EFS will roll out in phases starting fall 2024, initially with zero-data retention on Fable 5 and 5.1 for eligible customers, then transitioning to the full EFS offering. Support spans Claude's direct interface, Claude Code, Claude Enterprise, Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry.

The architecture reflects enterprise feedback on three points: monitoring must meet regulatory standards (Anthropic's automated systems flag patterns; customers decide what warrants investigation), data storage requires infrastructure customers already trust and control, and sensitive information like legal materials or drug-safety reports must stay under review by customer personnel only. This design lets enterprises deploy frontier models on regulated workflows—financial services, healthcare, law, telecom—where they couldn't before.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a concrete framework for enterprise AI governance at scale. For Applicative AI's consulting practice, EFS shows how to architect enterprise deployments that satisfy both security requirements and regulatory mandates—a pattern your clients face across financial services, healthcare, and government. For your teaching: this is how frontier model risks (autonomous misuse, credential theft, cyberattacks) translate into actual architectural controls, not just policies. The zero-data retention + monitoring split is a design principle you can extract for your own customer engagements. For India's AI ecosystem: as Indian enterprises and regulators start demanding similar controls on frontier models, understanding Anthropic's approach (worked out with US systemically important banks) becomes a reference point for domestic governance frameworks.
stories.potential_use: 1) Workshop module: walk through the enterprise security dilemma EFS solves (need for data retention vs. privacy constraints) and map the architecture choices Anthropic made; use this as a template for designing governance into AI deployments. 2) Consulting angle: audit your own client deployments against the three customer concerns Anthropic addressed (monitoring standards, storage trust, human review authority). 3) India angle: track if and how Indian financial regulators, healthcare bodies, and telecom operators adopt similar requirements; EFS may become a benchmark for what "responsible frontier AI deployment" looks like locally.

sources.title: Developing Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with our customers

stories.headline: BenchMIRT audits what LLM benchmarks actually measure, revealing hidden signals
stories.dek: Allen AI and Hugging Face release a multidimensional analysis tool that separates safety from reasoning signals in benchmark scores.
stories.summary:
Allen AI and Hugging Face have released BenchMIRT, a new method that applies multidimensional Item Response Theory to decode what individual benchmark questions actually measure. Trained on 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and 34,000+ questions, BenchMIRT independently recovered two dominant dimensions—safety and general reasoning—without being told which benchmarks were designed for which capability.

The analysis reveals that benchmark scores often mix multiple signals in ways that can obscure what they're really testing. BBQ, ostensibly a safety benchmark for social bias, actually aligns much more closely with general reasoning ability. WMDP, which tests dangerous dual-use knowledge, correlates more with reasoning than safety (though stronger reasoning predicts *lower* scores, since refusing the knowledge is the goal). HarmBench's copyright-violation questions cluster with reasoning, while its harmful-request questions cluster with safety—all folded into a single score.

BenchMIRT can also identify which questions best distinguish stronger from weaker models on each underlying capability. The researchers found that keeping just 10% of questions generally preserved the same capability ranking as the full benchmark, and 50% often matched even more closely. The tool can predict whether a model will answer an unseen question correctly 79% of the time, versus 70% for simpler baseline methods. Allen AI cautions that the method has limits: it works only on models trained through March 2025, the discovered dimensions depend on the benchmark set chosen, and the transparency into question-level details could theoretically be misused to weaken safety evaluations.
stories.why_it_matters: For an AI consultancy, benchmark literacy is operational: clients rely on benchmark scores to justify model choices, and misinterpreting what a score actually measures can lead to poor tooling decisions. BenchMIRT gives you a diagnostic framework to explain *why* a model scores well or poorly on a specific evaluation, moving beyond headline numbers. It's also highly relevant to AI education—teaching practitioners to audit benchmarks themselves prevents naive reliance on benchmark-driven marketing claims and builds the evaluation rigor your workshop participants need when assessing AI systems for real work.
stories.potential_use: Use BenchMIRT as a case study in your AI evaluation workshops: walk through how BBQ and HarmBench reveal mixed signals, then have participants pick a benchmark they use client-side and hypothesize what hidden dimensions might be lurking in its score. For consulting: when a client says "We need a model that scores high on X," ask which underlying capability they actually need (safety? reasoning? instruction-following?), and use BenchMIRT's logic to audit whether that benchmark measures it. Keep the 79% prediction accuracy statistic in your toolkit as evidence that benchmark questions aren't interchangeable—some carry far more signal than others.

sources.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

stories.headline: Empirik launches with $21M to predict infrastructure outages before they occur
stories.dek: The Sequoia-backed startup uses AI to track system changes and model their ripple effects, positioning itself as an autonomous traffic cop for DevOps teams.
stories.summary:
Empirik, spun out from Sequoia Capital's internal incubator, has raised $21 million in seed funding to commercialize a tool for preventing IT infrastructure failures. The company was built by Avon Puri, who spent over a decade running infrastructure at Rubrik and VMware before joining Sequoia as chief digital officer, and Sudheer Dhurjati, another Sequoia IT leader. They recognized that large language models could address a chronic pain point: most observability tools fail to understand how changes propagate through complex system dependencies.

The product works by tracking system changes and inferring their potential cascading effects across an entire infrastructure stack. Rather than waiting for incidents to occur, Empirik acts as what Sequoia describes as an autonomous "traffic cop"—automatically permitting low-risk changes, setting guardrails on medium-risk ones, and flagging dangerous updates for human review. This approach offloads routine troubleshooting from overextended DevOps and site reliability engineering teams, freeing them to tackle higher-value work.

The startup has moved quickly from incubation to market. Sequoia brought in Kartik Chandrayana, formerly chief product officer at Quantum Metric and observability VP at Salesforce, as CEO. Early customers already include S&P Global, Guardant Health, and a major CPG company. Chandrayana frames the opportunity as analogous to what Cursor and Claude Code achieved for software developers—automating repetitive tasks to accelerate human productivity in a field overwhelmed by constant change.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a concrete example of agentic AI solving a specific operational workflow problem at scale. For Applicative AI, it demonstrates a real use case where AI doesn't replace engineers but augments them by handling dependency analysis and routine decision-making at infrastructure scale—the kind of practical, bounded automation that clients across industries are actively seeking and paying for.
stories.potential_use: Use Empirik as a case study in workshops on operational AI applications—it illustrates how agentic systems can automate triage and low-stakes decisions while surfacing exceptions for human judgment. The pattern (track state, model consequences, flag for review) is transferable across domains and worth exploring with clients managing complex systems or distributed workflows.

sources.title: Sequoia-incubated Empirik launches with $21M to predict outages before they happen
